title: The Mechanic's Bench to the Aragon Steppe: Durruti, the Expropriations, and the Column
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: León, Santa Ana: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; both Wikipedia editions give 14 July 1896. The pin is the Plaza de Santa Ana per OpenStreetMap, the research pool's original figure sat 1.25 km north of the barrio and is corrected here.
stops.campa: In the barrio of Santa Ana, on the poor side of León, a son is born to Santiago Durruti, a railway worker on the Northern line, and Anastasia Dumange. They name him José Buenaventura. The father's wage feeds a house that will hold eight children, and the tracks are the one industry in the city that pays regularly, and they pay badly. The boy grows up inside the trade he will keep for life. He gives his occupation as mechanic in León, and goes on giving it in Paris, in Havana, in Buenos Aires, on forged papers and real ones.
sources: OpenStreetMap/Nominatim, Plaza de Santa Ana, León 24006
suggested_refs: The barrio de Santa Ana, León, and the workers' quarters of the Compañía de los Caminos de Hierro del Norte

stops.name: León, the tanners' strike and the father taken
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the León curtidores strike to 1903 and ties it to the family's hardship; the month of the arrest is not given, so the boy was six or seven depending on whether it fell before or after his birthday on 14 July. The day here orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The tanners of León strike for nine months and the city divides along the line the strike draws. Santiago Durruti takes the strikers' side and is arrested, and his son watches him taken. Whatever else the boy learns that year, he learns that the state comes to the door and removes the father, and he never revises it. He is six, or seven, depending which month of that long year the guards came. The household goes nine months short of the wage. He is out of school by eight and into the workshops.
stops.quote: Since my most tender age, the first thing I saw around me was suffering, not only in our family but also among our neighbors. Intuitively, I had already become a rebel. I think my fate was determined then.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister Rosa, quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The nine-month strike of the León curtidores, 1903

stops.name: León, the apprentice and the union card
stops.date_confidence: the apprenticeship under Melchor Martínez is dated 1910 by both Wikipedia editions and the UGT metalworkers' card to April 1913; the date here takes the earlier of the two to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is set to a mechanic's bench under Melchor Martínez, a socialist, who teaches him a trade and a politics in the same hours of the day. By April 1913 he carries a card in the metalworkers' union affiliated to the UGT and argues in its meetings against the older men who want the strike fund kept whole and the strike kept short. The Northern Railway takes him on as a mechanic, and by then he is already the kind of member who makes his own local uncomfortable. He has two employers, the company and the union.
stops.quote: Socialism is either active or isn't socialism.
stops.quote_source: Durruti in a union debate at León, quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The León metalworkers' section of the UGT, joined April 1913

stops.name: Matallana de Torío, the pumps and the strikers
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the Matallana pumps and his support of the striking miners to 1916; Abel Paz places related work at the La Robla mineral-washing shop from about 1912 and spreads the strike episode across 1913-1917, so the year orders a stretch rather than fixing a day. Coordinates corrected to the es.wikipedia figure for Matallana de Torío; two figures in the research pool were 6.5 and 13 km adrift.
stops.campa: He goes up the Torío valley to install mechanical pumps and mineral washers at the coal workings and finds the miners out on strike. The company needs his machines running. The strikers need the company squeezed. He does not assemble the washers. It is the first time he uses a skill as a weapon rather than as a wage. The UGT leadership in León counsels patience from a safe distance for the length of the dispute. He is nineteen or twenty, and he leaves them for good.
stops.quote: Mine managers need us to assemble our mineral washers as soon as possible because they're unable to keep up if we don't. But we're not budging. They have to choose between meeting the strikers' demands or disappointing their clients. It's up to them.
stops.quote_source: Quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution, on the La Robla mining conflict
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The La Robla mineral-washing workshop and the Matallana coal workings, León province

stops.name: León, the general strike of August 1917
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests his part in the revolutionary general strike of August 1917 and the loss of the railway job and expulsion from the Unión Ferroviaria that followed; the day given is the standard opening date of the strike and is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: The revolutionary general strike reaches the León depots and he is in it from the first day. The army breaks it in a week. The Northern Railway dismisses him and the Unión Ferroviaria expels him for defending revolutionary positions inside a union that has voted against them. At twenty-one he has no job, no card, and a file with the Civil Guard, who want to know who cut the telegraph wire and who put sand where oil should be. The conscription notice is already in the post.
suggested_refs: The revolutionary general strike of August 1917 and its repression on the northern railway lines

stops.name: Gijón, out from under the draft
stops.date_confidence: the flight north and out of Spain in December 1917 to escape conscription is attested by both editions; no day is given.
stops.campa: He goes north to the Asturian coast rather than to the barracks. The call-up would put him in the uniform of a king whose Civil Guard has just shot down the strike he helped run, and he does not present himself. He is a deserter from that day, and Spanish law in 1917 attaches no expiry to the condition and offers no amnesty out of it. From Gijón the road runs to the French frontier and he takes it. His name goes onto the list of prófugos kept in every provincial capital.
stops.quote: I was hardly excited to serve the homeland, and what scarce enthusiasm I had was taken from me by a sergeant who commanded the conscripts like they were already in the barracks. When I left the enlistment office, I declared that Alfonso XIII would have one less soldier and one more revolutionary.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister, quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The Gijón waterfront and the northern smuggling routes into France, 1917-1918

stops.name: San Sebastián, the court-martial for desertion
stops.date_confidence: the arrest at Santiago de Compostela is dated 1918 and the San Sebastián court-martial 1918-1919 in the reachable Wikipedia accounts; neither gives a month and neither states the sentence. The order of this episode relative to the La Felguera stretch is not fixed by any source consulted, and the day here orders the segment.
stops.campa: He is taken by the Civil Guard at Santiago de Compostela, where deserters gather because the Galician coast has boats, and brought east to San Sebastián to be court-martialed. He is twenty-one. What is attested is that he does not serve whatever he is given: he goes over the frontier into France on foot, through the same border country where his men will be ambushed six years later. How long the sentence ran, and whether it was even handed down before he went, is stated in no source consulted.
suggested_refs: The Guipúzcoa military jurisdiction at San Sebastián and its desertion caseload, 1918-1919

stops.name: La Felguera, the card of the CNT
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the formal CNT joining to January 1919 while he was working as a mechanic in La Felguera; the geography lens of the research pool gave 1918 for the same stretch, and the two are left unreconciled. A separate claim in the pool placing his CNT joining in Barcelona in 1920 is contradicted by both editions and is not followed. Coordinates corrected to the es.wikipedia figure.
stops.campa: In the metal town of La Felguera, at a mechanic's bench again, he signs the card of the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo. He is twenty-two, and he will hold that card until he dies under its initials seventeen years from now. The CNT is not a union that bargains and then goes home. It is a confederation that intends to take the factories, and its Asturian branches are full of men dismissed and blacklisted exactly as he was. The card costs a few céntimos a week.
stops.quote: The emancipation of the working class requires the complete destruction of capitalism and we can't stop our revolutionary efforts until that happens.
stops.quote_source: Quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The CNT of La Felguera and the Duro Felguera metalworks, Asturias

stops.name: Paris, the first exile
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia: by June 1919 he was working as a mechanic in Paris. The research pool attached the CNT joining to this stop, which is misplaced; he had joined at La Felguera in January.
stops.campa: By June he is twenty-two and working as a mechanic in Paris, one of the Spanish exiles who fill the shops of the eastern arrondissements, moving between French and Occitan cities as the work moves. He has a trade and a conviction behind him, and France asks after the first and not the second. France is also where the Spanish anarchist movement keeps its spare parts: printers, forgers, safe addresses, men who have already done what he is about to do.
suggested_refs: The Spanish exile colonies of eastern Paris and their anarchist press, 1919-1920

stops.name: San Sebastián, Los Justicieros and the king
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1920 by en.wikipedia, which names Manuel Buenacasa's branch, the uncovered plot against Alfonso XIII and the flight to Zaragoza by freight train. The research pool separately placed his CNT joining and the Riotinto support in Barcelona in 1920; en.wikipedia puts both in the north, and Barcelona does not become his base until 1922. No month is given.
stops.campa: Back on the Basque coast he joins the CNT branch that Manuel Buenacasa runs and helps form Los Justicieros, an affinity group of a dozen men who mean to kill Alfonso XIII. The plot is uncovered before it can be attempted. From the north that same year the group backs the Riotinto miners in Huelva by sabotage, at the opposite end of the country from the mine. He leaves the city in a freight wagon, riding it down to Zaragoza, where he takes work as a locksmith.
suggested_refs: Manuel Buenacasa's San Sebastián branch of the CNT and the affinity group Los Justicieros

stops.name: Eibar, the paymaster on the street
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the Eibar robbery to 1921 and names Gregorio Suberviola and Rafael Torres Escartín; the geography lens of the research pool dated the same event 1923. The two-year discrepancy is a lens error and is followed here in favour of the account that names the accomplices. No month is given.
stops.campa: With Gregorio Suberviola and Rafael Torres Escartín he takes a company paymaster on the street in Eibar, in the gun-making valley of Guipúzcoa. The money is not for them. Anarchist expropriation is a doctrine with a bookkeeping: the take pays for presses, for lawyers, for the families of prisoners, for pistols, and every peseta of it is argued over in meetings afterward. The Spanish press has a shorter word for the practice and prints it daily. The word is atraco.
suggested_refs: The Eibar armaments district of Guipúzcoa and the expropriation debates within the CNT, 1921-1923

stops.name: Barcelona, Los Solidarios and the grenade shop
stops.date_confidence: the founding of Los Solidarios is dated 1922 by es.wikipedia. The manufacture of some six thousand grenades with Eusebi Brau belongs to 1923, after March, per en.wikipedia; the research pool dated it 1922. It is folded into this stop for its place, not for its date. The Bilbao arms-buying trip is tagged [R] in the pool.
stops.campa: In Barcelona, in the years when the employers' pistoleros and the CNT gunmen are killing each other at a rate of one a week, he founds Los Solidarios with Juan García Oliver, Francisco Ascaso and Ricardo Sanz. Ascaso becomes the nearest thing to a brother he has. What the group is arming for is not defence but a rising it expects to call itself. They buy weapons in Bilbao, and in an underground workshop with the Catalan metalworker Eusebi Brau they turn out some six thousand grenades.
suggested_refs: Los Solidarios, Barcelona 1922-1923, and the pistolerismo of the Catalan employers' federation

stops.name: Madrid, Calle de Alcalá: the arrest
stops.date_confidence: the April 1923 arrest on the Calle de Alcalá is attested by en.wikipedia; no day is given. The tripartite charge of armed robbery, attempted regicide and desertion, and the acquittal on the first two counts, appear in the research pool but in neither Wikipedia edition, and are reported here as report rather than as fact. Abel Paz would have to be checked before they are stated flat.
stops.campa: He comes to Madrid in April to see comrades held in the Modelo and is arrested on the Calle de Alcalá, in the open, in the middle of the capital, at twenty-six. Three charges are said to have been laid: armed robbery, the attempted killing of the king, desertion. No paperwork for any of the three has ever been produced. Whatever was charged, the detention is short, because by the first of September he is at liberty in Gijón with a pistol in his coat.
suggested_refs: The Modelo prison of Madrid and the CNT prisoners held there in the spring of 1923

stops.name: Zaragoza, the cardinal in the car
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The date and the killing are attested. The attribution to Los Solidarios is what the press asserted and what later historiography repeats; no source consulted establishes Durruti's personal part, and both lenses of the research pool flagged the distinction. Retained as reconstruction and not resolved.
stops.campa: Cardinal Juan Soldevila y Romero, Archbishop of Zaragoza, is shot dead in his car outside the city on the fourth of June. The press names Los Solidarios the same week and the naming sticks. It is read as the answer to the killing of Salvador Seguí in Barcelona ten weeks earlier, one gun for another. No court establishes who fired, and nobody who was present has ever named the man who did. The attribution to Durruti has been repeated for a century without once closing.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Cardinal Soldevila y Romero, 4 June 1923, and the killing of Salvador Seguí in March of the same year

stops.name: Gijón, the Bank of Spain
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 September 1923 by en.wikipedia, including the sum, the manager's resistance and the grazing shot.
stops.campa: Four men walk into the Gijón branch of the Bank of Spain and leave with six hundred and fifty thousand pesetas, money earmarked for getting imprisoned comrades out. The manager fights. He bites Durruti, he slaps him, and a bullet grazes his neck in the struggle. The León papers will print escapes that never happened, and the Durruti gang becomes a name police in three provinces attach to robberies nobody in it committed. Afterward the party goes up into a mountain cabin and waits there.
suggested_refs: The Banco de España branch at Gijón, robbed 1 September 1923

segments.name: Los Errantes: the Latin American Circuit

stops.name: Paris, Belleville and the Renault bench
stops.date_confidence: the flight to Paris with Ascaso is dated November 1923 and the Renault work and Belleville residence 1924 by en.wikipedia; the date here orders the segment.
stops.campa: With Ascaso he crosses into France in November, after Gijón, and settles in Belleville, the quarter where the Spanish exiles live six to a room. He takes a mechanic's job at Renault and works it like any immigrant workman: shifts, wages, a landlord. The room is a mail drop, an armoury and a debating society at once. The Primo de Rivera dictatorship is a few months old and everyone on the staircase has a plan for ending it. He draws his pay under a name that is not his.
suggested_refs: The Belleville quarter of Paris and its Spanish anarchist exile community, 1923-1926

stops.name: Hendaye and Bera, the ambush at the frontier
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1924 by en.wikipedia, which gives the ambush and the two dead without naming a day; the day here orders the segment.
stops.campa: He leads a party of exiles down to the Bidasoa to cross at Hendaye and take the barracks at Bera on the Spanish side, the opening move of a rising that is supposed to spread from the border inward. He is twenty-eight. The guards know they are coming. Two of the men are killed at the frontier and the rest scatter back into France, where the police now want him nearly as badly as the Spanish do. He does not carry a rifle into Spain again for eleven years.
suggested_refs: The Vera de Bidasoa incursion of November 1924 against the Primo de Rivera dictatorship

stops.name: Havana, the docks
stops.date_confidence: the embarkation for Cuba with Ascaso on false passports is dated December 1924 by en.wikipedia; no day is given.
stops.campa: He and Ascaso ship out for Cuba on false passports and land in Havana with no money and a trade. The Latin American years begin as ordinary emigration, the same passage thousands of Galicians and Asturians are making in the same months for the same reason. Inside a season it becomes a two-year circuit of organizing and armed expropriation across five countries, financed by the banks of each country in turn. Meanwhile he works the docks, where the heat is worse than anything in Asturias and the pay is better.
suggested_refs: The Havana waterfront unions and the Spanish emigrant passage to Cuba, 1924-1925

stops.name: Santa Clara, the note signed Los Errantes
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia places the sugarcane strike, the killing of the employer and the note signed Los Errantes in Santa Clara province in 1925; the geography lens of the research pool gave 1924-1925 for the same stretch. No month is given.
stops.campa: In the cane country of Santa Clara they cut sugar and organize the cutters. During a strike the employer is killed and a note is left on the body, signed Los Errantes, the wanderers. It is the name they use in the Americas and it is accurate: from here the group moves constantly, a week ahead of a police telegram that never gains on them and never quite stops. They have no country to be deported to that would not hang them. Nothing in the record says which of them wrote the note, or which of them fired.
suggested_refs: The Cuban sugar strikes of 1925 and the anarchist groups of Santa Clara province

stops.name: Mexico City, the Confederación General de Trabajadores
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the reunion with Alejandro Ascaso and Gregorio Jover in Mexico City to March 1925; the Yucatán landing, the Tecomán robbery and the Tampico lectures are attested to 1925 without months and are folded here for place.
stops.campa: They come ashore in Yucatán after bribing the Treasury officers on the pier, and reach the capital, where the General Confederation of Workers takes them in. Mexico is the one country on the circuit with a labour movement strong enough to shelter them openly. Alejandro Ascaso and Gregorio Jover join them there. At Tampico Durruti lectures on rationalist education, the schooling Francisco Ferrer was shot for in Barcelona sixteen years earlier. With local anarchists they rob an office at Tecomán.
suggested_refs: The Confederación General de Trabajadores of Mexico and the Ferrer-style rationalist schools of Tampico

stops.name: Valparaíso, the Bank of Chile
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia has the group reaching Valparaíso in May 1925 and robbing the Bank of Chile branch in July; no day is given. The claim that this was the first anarchist bank robbery in Chilean history is supported by neither Wikipedia edition and is reported as claim. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave a positive latitude, which plots in the Syrian desert.
stops.campa: The group has been in the city since May. In the port they take a branch of the Bank of Chile. The Chilean press calls it unprecedented, and the claim that it is the first anarchist bank robbery in the country's history enters the literature and stays there, repeated ever since without a citation anyone has produced. What is certain is the money and the direction it travels: to the movement's prisoners and presses in Europe, carried by hand over the Andes and across the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: The Banco de Chile branch at Valparaíso, robbed July 1925

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the port and the wanted poster
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925 by en.wikipedia for both the dockwork in Buenos Aires and the robbery at San Martín on the city's edge; no months are given, and the date orders the segment. Coordinates are the canonical atlas pin for Buenos Aires; the research pool's positive latitudes for Buenos Aires and San Martín were sign errors.
stops.campa: Buenos Aires becomes the centre of the group's operations and he works the docks among the Spanish and Italian stevedores of a port where the anarchist unions still set the pace. La Protesta is printed in this city. So are the wanted posters with his face on them, which go up within weeks of his arrival and put an end to the dockwork. To pay for the passage back to Europe they rob a bank at San Martín, on the edge of the city, and take ship in February for France.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires waterfront, La Protesta, and the FORA in the mid-1920s

segments.name: La Santé, and the Years Without a Country

stops.name: Paris, La Santé
stops.date_confidence: the arrest of 25 June 1926 after an informer betrayed a plot against Alfonso XIII during a royal visit, and the imprisonment in La Santé, are attested by en.wikipedia; coordinates corrected to the fr.wikipedia figure for the prison at 42 rue de la Santé. The remark on Bakunin and Kropotkin is undated in Abel Paz and is placed here for the prison years, not attested to them.
stops.campa: An informer sells the plan. Alfonso XIII is to visit Paris and is to be killed there, and on the twenty-fifth of June Durruti, Ascaso and Jover are arrested and put in La Santé, where they will stay for a year. He is thirty and has never held a position of any kind. There is time in a cell to read, and what he says about his reading is a workman's judgement on two masters rather than a disciple's. Mikhail Bakunin gives him the destruction. Kropotkin gives him the morning after.
stops.quote: Their perspectives help balance one another: there is violence and radicalism in Bakunin, whereas one finds a practical element and the foundations of the free society in Kropotkin.
stops.quote_source: Durruti on Bakunin and Kropotkin, quoted in Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: La Santé prison, 42 rue de la Santé, Paris 14e

stops.name: Paris, the hunger strike and the gate
stops.date_confidence: the trial at the Palais de Justice on 7 October 1926, the hunger strike begun 13 February 1927 against extradition to Argentina, and the release on 8 July 1927 after Louis Lecoin's campaign secured a majority in the Chamber of Deputies, are all attested by en.wikipedia. Three dated events are folded into one stop; the date is the release.
stops.campa: At the Palais de Justice in October he confesses to the charge and explains it: what the Primo de Rivera dictatorship does in Spain is what he answers for in Paris. Then Argentina asks for him, and Argentina still shoots anarchists. On the thirteenth of February he stops eating. Inside La Santé that is the whole of what he can do about it. Outside, Louis Lecoin runs a campaign that turns a majority of the Chamber of Deputies against the extradition. On the eighth of July the gate opens and he walks out with nothing.
stops.quote: we're going to continue the struggle with even greater intensity
stops.quote_source: Durruti on his release from prison, Paris, 8 July 1927, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Buenaventura Durruti'
suggested_refs: Louis Lecoin's 1927 campaign against the extradition of Durruti, Ascaso and Jover

stops.name: Ménilmontant, the bookshop
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Reported from Wikipedia by the research pool and tagged reconstruction there. The bookshop meeting with Émilienne Morin and Nestor Makhno is movement tradition and no primary source for it was reached; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: In an anarchist bookshop in Ménilmontant, in the months after his release, he meets two people. One is Nestor Makhno, who commanded a peasant army across the Ukrainian steppe, lost it to the Bolsheviks, and is living out his exile in Paris as a stagehand and a carpenter. The other is Émilienne Morin, a French anarchist and a stenographer, who becomes his companion for the rest of his life. Neither meeting is documented outside the accounts the movement keeps of itself.
suggested_refs: The anarchist bookshops of Ménilmontant and Belleville, Paris, in the later 1920s

stops.name: Berlin, sheltered and expelled
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the Berlin sheltering by Augustin Souchy and Rudolf Rocker to 1928 and the expulsion after objections by the Centre Party to 1929; the research pool merged the two under one year and they are separated here. The attendance at an IWA congress is tagged [R] in the pool and no primary source for it was reached. No months are given.
stops.campa: Expelled from France, he is taken in at Berlin by Augustin Souchy and Rudolf Rocker, who between them run the international of anarcho-syndicalism out of an office and a typewriter. He attends a congress of the International Workers' Association. He is thirty-two, with a warrant waiting at home and no country obliged to keep him. Germany does not keep him either: the Centre Party objects to the presence of a Spanish gunman, and in 1929 he is put out.
suggested_refs: The Berlin secretariat of the International Workers' Association under Rudolf Rocker and Augustin Souchy

stops.name: Brussels, La Voz de Libertaria
stops.date_confidence: the Brussels years, the metalworking job and the founding of La Voz de Libertaria are dated 1929-1931 by en.wikipedia; no months are given and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Belgium tolerates him. He finds work as a metalworker in Brussels and helps set up a paper, La Voz de Libertaria, printed for the Spanish exiles scattered across northern Europe. Émilienne Morin is with him. For two years he lives the life of a skilled emigrant workman with a police file: shifts, rent, a paper to get out on time, and the Spanish news read closely every morning, because the dictatorship is visibly failing and the exiles are counting the months.
suggested_refs: La Voz de Libertaria, Brussels, 1929-1931

segments.name: The Republic That Keeps Arresting Him

stops.name: Barcelona, the fourteenth of April
stops.date_confidence: the return among the first anarchist exiles is tied to the proclamation of the Second Republic on 14 April 1931 by en.wikipedia; whether he crossed the frontier that day or in the days following is not fixed.
stops.campa: The king leaves, the Second Republic is proclaimed on the fourteenth of April, and Durruti is on a southbound train inside the week, among the first exiles back. He has been out of Spain, with short returns, for most of eight years. Nobody in the city yet knows what a republic run by republicans intends to do about the unions that made it possible. In April 1931 the CNT can hold a public meeting in Barcelona for the first time since the dictatorship closed its halls.
suggested_refs: The amnesty of April 1931 and the return of the anarchist exiles to Catalonia

stops.name: Montjuïc, the CNT meeting on the hill
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the Montjuïc CNT meeting to 19 April 1931; the geography lens of the research pool gave 18 or 19 April for the same meeting. The prediction of civil war is reported in both.
stops.campa: Five days after the proclamation he speaks to a CNT meeting on the hill of Montjuïc, under the fortress whose guns have been turned on the city more than once. The meeting is full of men who came home in April on the same amnesty he did. He is out by five years and three months. The change of regime, he tells them, is a step toward democratization, and a step is all it is. If the new government ignores what the working class is asking for, there will be civil war.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Montjuïc and the CNT mass meetings of spring 1931

stops.name: Barcelona, the bed of the truck
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens of the research pool places this at a May Day rally of over 100,000; the geography lens places the truck speech outside the Palau de la Generalitat after the Civil Guard fired on demonstrators. Almost certainly one episode differently located; the contradiction is left open and the Generalitat pin used.
stops.campa: May Day brings more than a hundred thousand people into the streets and the Civil Guard fires on them. Durruti climbs onto the bed of a truck and talks the crowd down. He has been back in the country five weeks, and the government's own file on him would not have predicted this. The two accounts of the day disagree about where he was standing, outside the Palau de la Generalitat or in the body of the rally, and neither is preferred here. Both have the shooting, and both have him up on the truck.
suggested_refs: The May Day demonstration of 1931 in Barcelona and the Civil Guard's response

stops.name: Barcelona, Colette born
stops.date_confidence: the birth date of 4 December 1931 is attested by fr.wikipedia's article on Émilienne Morin and agreed by en.wikipedia. No source states the city. The research pool gave Paris, which is unsupported: Durruti and Morin had returned to Spain in April 1931 and he is documented in Catalonia through December. Barcelona is inference, not attestation. The Girona arrest is dated only to December 1931.
stops.campa: They have been together four years. Colette Durruti is born to Émilienne Morin on the fourth of December, their only child. He is thirty-five and has a daughter in a city where his name is back on the police lists. The shape of the Republic's five years is set by now: at liberty long enough to organize, then detained, then released, then detained again, with Colette raised mostly by her mother in the gaps. Later the same month he is arrested at Girona railway station.
suggested_refs: Émilienne Morin, stenographer and anarchist, and the Girona station arrest of December 1931

stops.name: Barcelona, the steamer Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: the Fígols rising in the Alt Llobregat is January 1932 and en.wikipedia dates the sailing of the merchant steamer Buenos Aires with its preventive prisoners to the morning of 10 February 1932, bound for Bata in Spanish Guinea, with the party later moved to the Canaries and back in Spain by September. The research pool merged this deportation with the December 1933 arrest under a single date; the two are twenty-two months apart and are kept apart here.
stops.campa: The miners of Fígols in the Alt Llobregat take their valley in January and declare libertarian communism inside it for five days. The Republic puts it down and deports the men it blames, Durruti among them, with no trial and no sentence. The Republic has now exiled him as the monarchy did. On the morning of the tenth of February the merchant steamer Buenos Aires sails from Barcelona for Spanish Guinea with a hold of preventive prisoners. They are moved on to the Canaries and are home by September.
suggested_refs: The Alt Llobregat insurrection of January 1932 and the deportations to Bata, Spanish Guinea

stops.name: Barcelona, the December insurrection
stops.date_confidence: attested to the afternoon of 13 December 1933 by es.wikipedia, following the anarcho-syndicalist insurrection of that month. The research pool attached the 1932 Guinea deportation to this date; no Guinea deportation followed the December 1933 arrest.
stops.campa: On the afternoon of the thirteenth of December he is arrested in Barcelona after the anarcho-syndicalist insurrection of that month, the CNT's answer to elections that have just returned the right. The rising fails everywhere it is tried and is put down inside a week. The arithmetic of the Republic is familiar to him by now: each insurrection costs the confederation its organizers for six months and gains it nothing anyone can point to on a map. He is thirty-seven, and he is inside again.
suggested_refs: The anarchist insurrection of December 1933 and the CNT prisoners of the bienio negro

stops.name: Barcelona, the nineteenth of July
stops.date_confidence: his part in the anarchist defeat of the military rising in Barcelona on 19 July 1936 is attested in both Wikipedia editions. The quotation is from the Pierre van Paassen interview published 24 July 1936 and its exact wording and attribution are disputed among researchers; it is carried as tradition, not as a verified transcript.
stops.campa: The garrison rises on the nineteenth and the workers of Barcelona break it in the streets in a day and a half, with pistols, cobblestones and the rifles taken out of the first barracks stormed. Durruti is in it from the first hour. What a union does with a city it has won is a question nobody in the CNT has answered. By the twentieth the army in Catalonia has been beaten by the CNT and the FAI, and the men who did it hold the arsenals, the factories, the trams and the telephone exchange.
stops.quote: We carry a new world here, in our hearts.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Durruti in the Pierre van Paassen interview, Toronto Star, 24 July 1936; wording and attribution disputed among researchers
suggested_refs: The defeat of the military rising in Barcelona, 19-20 July 1936

stops.name: Palau de la Generalitat, before Companys
stops.date_confidence: the meeting with Lluís Companys at which the CNT delegation put a military committee rather than a government is standardly dated 20 July 1936, the day the rising was finally crushed in Barcelona; the research pool's chronology lens gave 21 July. Ascaso's death at the Atarazanas barracks on 20 July is standard in the historiography of the rising and is stated on that basis, not from a source reached directly for this file. The quotation is from the disputed van Paassen interview.
stops.campa: Armed and unwashed, the CNT delegation walks into the Palau de la Generalitat to see Lluís Companys, who tells them they are masters of the city and asks what they intend to do with it. Durruti and García Oliver put to him a military committee rather than a government. That same day Francisco Ascaso is killed storming the Atarazanas barracks, thirteen years after the two of them took the Bank of Spain at Gijón together. Durruti goes to the front without him.
stops.quote: No government fights fascism to destroy it.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Durruti in the Pierre van Paassen interview, 24 July 1936; some researchers suggest embellishment or fabrication
suggested_refs: The Palau de la Generalitat meeting of 20 July 1936 and the Central Committee of Antifascist Militias

stops.name: Bujaraloz, la Casa de Rozas
stops.date_confidence: the column left Barcelona on 24 July 1936 and es.wikipedia's article on Bujaraloz records its arrival on 25 July with the headquarters at la Casa de Rozas; the research pool dated the Aragon offensive to August, a week and more late. Coordinates confirmed against the es.wikipedia figure. The Koltsov quotation is secondhand from Hugh Thomas and was not checked against Koltsov's diary.
stops.campa: The column leaves Barcelona on the twenty-fourth, some two thousand men and women in requisitioned lorries with a black and red flag on the cab, and reaches Bujaraloz on the steppe the next day. He puts his headquarters in a farmhouse, la Casa de Rozas, on the road to Zaragoza. There is no artillery. There is no regular officer except those who have chosen to come, and whether that is the entire point or the reason Zaragoza will hold gets argued from the first week. The column elects its delegates and votes on its orders.
stops.quote: It is possible that only a hundred of us will survive, but with that hundred we shall enter Saragossa.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Durruti in an interview with Mikhail Koltsov, July 1936, cited secondhand in Hugh Thomas, The Spanish Civil War
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: La Casa de Rozas at Bujaraloz, headquarters of the Durruti Column on the Aragon front

stops.name: Pina de Ebro, the deeds burned
stops.date_confidence: the collectivizations along the Ebro through the summer of 1936 are attested in the standard accounts and Abel Paz is the source the research pool used for Pina de Ebro specifically; no day is given. Coordinates corrected: the pool's longitude put the stop 21 km out in open steppe. The quotation is widely attributed to an interview of 3 October 1936 and was not confirmed verbatim in any primary text reached.
stops.campa: The column takes the villages along the Ebro and in each one the land is collectivized: the deeds burned, the fields worked in common, money in some places abolished outright in favour of a ration book. Not every village wants it, and where a village does not want it the column's own accounts admit that it is imposed anyway. War and revolution are being run out of the same lorries. He has said in public that he will not postpone the second until the first is finished.
stops.quote: The pickaxe and the shovel are as important as the rifle.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Durruti, cited in the secondary literature to an interview of 3 October 1936; not confirmed verbatim in any primary text reached
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
suggested_refs: The Aragon collectives of 1936-1937 along the Ebro

stops.name: Perdiguera, the line that stops
stops.date_confidence: the column's position at Perdiguera on the line toward Zaragoza, and its lack of the artillery needed to take the city, are attested by Wikipedia and Abel Paz for the late summer and autumn of 1936; no day is given. Coordinates corrected to the es.wikipedia figure, 9.5 km from the pool's. The quotation is Emma Goldman's report of his answer to a militiaman and is verbatim from her essay.
stops.campa: The line stops at Perdiguera, short of Zaragoza, and does not move again. The column has rifles and lorries and nothing that will break a fortified city, and the Republic's war ministry, which has the artillery, is not sending it to an anarchist column that refuses to be militarized. So they dig, and the autumn comes down early on the steppe. Men who joined in July to take Zaragoza in a week are still in the same trenches in September, and some of them want to go home for the harvest.
stops.quote: All right, but you will go on foot, and by the time you reach your village, everybody will know that your courage had failed you, that you have run away, that you have shirked your self-imposed task.
stops.quote_source: Emma Goldman, 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living' (1936), reporting his answer to a militiaman who asked to leave
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution
Emma Goldman, 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living', Spain and the World (1936)
suggested_refs: The Aragon front line at Perdiguera and the militarization dispute of autumn 1936

stops.name: Bujaraloz, Emma Goldman at the headquarters
stops.date_confidence: Goldman visited the Aragon front and the Durruti Column in the autumn of 1936 and published 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living' after his death; the essay does not fix the date or the exact place of the interview, and the Bujaraloz pin is used because it was the column's headquarters. The quotation is verbatim from the text on theanarchistlibrary.org, in Goldman's two-sentence punctuation, which the research pool had rendered as a comma splice.
stops.campa: Emma Goldman comes to the Aragon front and interviews him at the column's headquarters. She has been an anarchist for forty-seven years and has watched one revolution she believed in harden into a state; she has come to Spain to see whether it can be done otherwise. She goes back to England and writes it up while he is still alive. He talks to her about discipline, which he says must be inner discipline, and about the volunteers who came to him without conscription and may leave when they choose.
stops.quote: I have been an Anarchist all my life. I hope I have remained one. I should consider it very sad indeed, had I to turn into a general and rule the men with a military rod.
stops.quote_source: Emma Goldman, 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living', Spain and the World (1936), quoting her interview with him at the Aragon front
sources: Emma Goldman, 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living', Spain and the World (1936), full text at theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: Emma Goldman's 1936 visit to the Aragon front and her essay 'Durruti Is Dead, Yet Living'

stops.name: Ciudad Universitaria, the column committed
stops.date_confidence: the column's move from Aragon to Madrid and its commitment at the Ciudad Universitaria are attested to mid-November 1936 in both editions; the day given orders the segment. Casualty figures differ between accounts and none is stated here as fixed.
stops.campa: Madrid is being taken street by street and the government has left for Valencia. Durruti brings part of his column up from Aragon in the middle of November on the argument that Madrid holds or everything is lost. They are put into the Ciudad Universitaria, where the front runs through lecture halls and the Clinical Hospital changes hands floor by floor. His men are not trained for this kind of fighting. Within days the column is cut to pieces, and the accounts do not agree on how badly.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Ciudad Universitaria, Madrid, November 1936

stops.name: Calle de Isaac Peral, the shot
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the mechanism. The wounding on 19 November 1936 is attested. es.wikipedia names the Calle Isaac Peral; en.wikipedia's article on his death does not name the street and places the wounding near the Hospital Clínico. The accidental-discharge account belongs to his secretary Jesús Arnal, from 1967, not to the driver, as the research pool had it: the driver Julio Graves reported enemy fire. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim figure for the street.
stops.campa: Less than two hours after giving an interview he is shot through the chest on the Calle de Isaac Peral. Who fired has never been established. His driver, Julio Graves, said the fire came from the Clinical Hospital, which the Nationalists held. His secretary, Jesús Arnal, said decades afterward that the safety on Durruti's own naranjero slipped and the open-bolt gun went off against him. Others have said a fifth columnist, or men he stopped from running, or the NKVD.
sources: Nominatim, Calle de Isaac Peral, Madrid 28015
suggested_refs: Jesús Arnal's 1967 account of the shooting, and Julio Graves's contrary account

stops.name: Hotel Ritz, the blood hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia gives the death at four in the morning of 20 November 1936 in the Hotel Ritz, converted into a blood hospital for the Catalan militias, and cites the autopsy for the nine-millimetre wound. The judgements of Abel Paz and Helen Graham are reported from the English Wikipedia article on his death.
stops.campa: He dies at four in the morning in the Hotel Ritz, which the Catalan militias have turned into a blood hospital, of a nine-millimetre wound through the epigastrium that took the spleen and the diaphragm. He is forty years old. The autopsy is performed and recorded. Abel Paz, who gave decades to the question, concluded that the true circumstances of the shot remain an enigma, and Helen Graham calls the accidental-discharge account compelling without calling it settled.
sources: Abel Paz, Durruti en la revolución española
suggested_refs: The Hotel Ritz of Madrid as a militia blood hospital, and the autopsy report of 20 November 1936

stops.name: Via Laietana, the procession
stops.date_confidence: attested to 23 November 1936 by the English Wikipedia article on his death, which gives the embalming in Madrid and a crowd estimated between 200,000 and 500,000 and describes the funeral as the largest in Spanish history.
stops.campa: The body is embalmed in Madrid and brought back to Barcelona, and on the twenty-third the city stops. Somewhere between two hundred thousand and half a million people fill Via Laietana and the streets feeding into it, in a city of a million and a little more. It is called the largest funeral in Spanish history, and nobody who was there and wrote about it afterward disputed the description. The coffin moves at walking pace behind the militia bands, down the same street where the CNT has its headquarters and where the fighting began in July.
suggested_refs: The funeral procession of 23 November 1936 down Via Laietana, Barcelona

stops.name: Columbus Monument, the four eulogies
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia's article on his death names four speakers at the Columbus Monument: the Soviet consul Volodymyr Antonov-Ovseenko, President Lluís Companys, Justice Minister Joan Garcia Oliver and Health Minister Federica Montseny. The research pool listed only two. The consul's presence is noted because the same article records an NKVD theory of the shooting.
stops.campa: At the foot of the Columbus Monument the coffin is set down and four people speak over it: the Soviet consul Antonov-Ovseenko, President Lluís Companys of Catalonia, the CNT justice minister Joan Garcia Oliver, and the health minister Federica Montseny. The man who spent his life refusing to enter a government is buried by two ministers of one, in the presence of the representative of the state that is arming the Republic and will shortly help break the CNT.
suggested_refs: The eulogies at the Columbus Monument, Barcelona, 23 November 1936

stops.name: Montjuïc Cemetery, plot 69
stops.date_confidence: the procession was 23 November 1936 and the interment 24 November, delayed by rain, per the English Wikipedia article on his death; the research pool gave 22 November for the burial, a date attested for neither event. Coordinates are the ca.wikipedia figure for the Cementiri de Montjuïc, replacing a pool figure 2.2 km adrift. The Friends of Durruti group was constituted in March 1937, before the May Days, not during them.
stops.campa: Rain puts the burial off by a day. He goes into plot 69 at Montjuïc on the twenty-fourth. In March 1937 veterans of his column take his name for a group, the Friends of Durruti, and use it against the militarization he had held off. The Communist press meanwhile circulates a story that his own comrades shot him at the Modelo, which the Madrid wound and the burial timetable both contradict. In 1937 he is moved into a shared grave, agrupación 13a, beside Francisco Ascaso and near the cenotaph of Francesc Ferrer i Guàrdia.
suggested_refs: The shared grave at agrupación 13a, Cementiri de Montjuïc, and the Agrupación de los Amigos de Durruti, March 1937
